summaries.summary: Natural Language Generation (NLG) in Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS) converts Dialogue Manager meaning representations into utterances, while conventional approaches rely on hand-tuned templates and rules.
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) show promise for NLG, but require annotated datasets for dialogue acts (DAs) and use DA conditioning, heuristic gates, or SC-LSTM.
Encoder-Decoder networks, especially attentional models and Attentional RNN Encoder-Decoder (ARED), have been explored for NLG and improved other tasks.
The proposed ARED extension introduces RALSTM on the decoder side, learns from unaligned data, and outperformed state-of-the-art methods on four NLG domains in BLEU and slot error rate ERR scores.
The paper outlines related work, the proposed model, experiments, results and analysis, and conclusion and future work sections.
RNNs-based models have shown promising NLG performance and have been applied to Chinese poetry, image captioning, conversational modeling, and machine translation.
Task-oriented dialogue generators include BIBREF3, SC-LSTM, and an out-of-domain model using counterfeited data and fine tuning with small in-domain data.
RNN encoder-decoder models with attention improved various tasks, including review networks, two attention layers, and attentive slot-value pair generators with domain scalability.
Open domain dialogue systems should use existing abilities from other domains, and prior works address multi-domain dialogue state tracking, adaptation steps, and SDS component adaptation.
The recurrent language generator has an Encoder, an Aligner, and an RNN Decoder that encode MR inputs, align semantic elements, and generate lexicalizable token sequences.
The encoder uses separated slots and values parameters to embed source information into a vector representation z_i.
Equation 10 defines z_i as the concatenation of u_i and v_i.
A 1-layer Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) encodes L slot-value pair embeddings into forward and backward hidden states summed into E.
Equation 12 defines e_i as the sum of forward and backward hidden states.
The Aligner uses an attention mechanism to calculate the DA representation.
Equation 14 defines beta_t,i using exponentials of e_t,i normalized over j.
The paragraph introduces the definition where e_t,i is specified.
Equation 15 defines e_t,i as a(e_i, h_t-1).
beta_t,i is the attention weight of the i-th slot-value pair, and the alignment model a is computed.
Equation 16 defines a(e_i, h_t-1) using v_a, W_a, U_a, tanh, and e_i and h_t-1.
v_a, W_a, and U_a are learned weight matrices, and the Aligner calculates dialogue act embedding d_t.
Equation 17 defines d_t as a concatenated with the weighted sum of beta_t,i e_i.
a is the vector embedding of the action type.
The semantic RALSTM cell for the Decoder side consists of a Refinement cell, a traditional LSTM cell, and an Adjustment cell.
Instead of feeding original input token w_t into the RNN cell, the input is recomputed using a semantic gate.
Equation 19 defines r_t and x_t using W_rd, W_rh, d_t, h_t-1, and element-wise multiplication with w_t.
The Refinement gate r_t refines w_t using d_t and h_t-1, with W_rh acting like a key phrase detector.
The traditional LSTM network from BIBREF26 introduces input gate i_i, forget gate f_t, and output gates o_t to control information flow.
Equation 20 computes i_t, f_t, o_t, and c-hat_t using sigmoids, tanh, W_4n,4n, x_t, d_t, and h_t-1.
n is hidden layer size, W_4n,4n is model parameters, and cell memory c_t depends on the DA representation.
Equation 21 modifies c_t with W_cr r_t and computes tilde-h_t from o_t and tanh(c_t).
tilde-h_t is the output.
An additional gating cell on top of the traditional LSTM gates controlling vector s, starting from 1-hot DA vector s_0 and using LSTM output tilde-h_t.
Equation 22 defines a_t and s_t using W_ax, W_ah, x_t, tilde-h_t, and element-wise multiplication with s_t-1.
W_ax and W_ah are learned weight matrices, a_t is the Adjustment gate, and an additional output uses o_t on remaining s_t information.
Equation 23 computes c_a and tilde-h_a using W_os, s_t, o_t, and tanh.
W_os projects the DA presentation into output space, tilde-h_a is the Adjustment cell output, and final RALSTM output combines both cell outputs.
Equation 24 defines h_t as tilde-h_t plus tilde-h_a.
The output distribution is computed by applying a softmax function g and can be sampled to obtain the next token.
Equation 25 defines P(w_t+1 | w_t,...w_0, DA) using g(W_ho h_t) and samples w_t+1 from that distribution.
DA is defined as (s, z).
The objective function was the negative log-likelihood.
Equation 27 defines F(theta) as the negative sum over T of y_t transpose log p_t.

Generators were trained with each sentence as a mini-batch, l_2 regularization every 5 training examples, pretrained Glove word embedding vectors, stochastic gradient descent, back propagation through time, and early stopping.
Decoding has over-generation and reranking phases, with beam search generating candidate responses and generator cost forming reranking score R.
Equation 29 defines R as F(theta) plus lambda ERR.
lambda is a large trade off constant penalizing nonsensical outputs, and slot error rate ERR counts missing or redundant generated slots.
Equation 30 defines ERR as (p + q) divided by N.
N is the total number of slots in DA, and p and q are the numbers of missing and redundant slots.
Experiments assessed the proposed models using several metrics, datasets, and model architectures to compare with prior methods.
The models were assessed on four NLG domains, with Restaurant and Hotel from BIBREF4 and harder Laptop and TV datasets from BIBREF22.
Generators used TensorFlow, a 3:1:1 split, hidden layer size 80, beam size 10, 70% dropout, 5 runs, early stopping, BLEU-based selection, λ 1000, 20 candidates, top 5 realizations, and four analyses.
Generator performance was assessed using BLEU and slot error rate ERR with an open source benchmark toolkit, against three state-of-the-art NLG baselines.
HLSTM proposed by BIBREF3 thwsjy15 used a heuristic gate to ensure all slot-value information was accurately captured during generation.
SCLSTM proposed by BIBREF4 wensclstm15 can jointly learn the gating signal and language model.
Enc-Dec proposed by BIBREF8 wentoward applied the attention-based encoder-decoder architecture.
Extensive experiments showed the proposed models consistently achieved better performance on both evaluation metrics across all domains in all test cases.
Ablation studies showed Adjustment cell reduces slot error rate ERR, ARED-based models improve BLEU and reduce ERR by about 2% to 4%, and gated models outperform SCLSTM.
Figure 3 shows RALSTM outperformed Enc-Dec and SCLSTM on unseen laptop domain from 1% to 100% training data, while Enc-Dec had much greater ERR.
Table 4 shows RALSTM and All2* generated appropriate, more complete, and concise sentences, while previous models produced missing and misplaced information errors.
The results prove the Refinement cell aggregates and selects attentive information, and the Adjustment cell controls the feature vector.
Figure 4 shows RALSTM outperformed Enc-Dec and SCLSTM on all domains in BLEU and ERR, while Enc-Dec struggled to reduce ERR.
Figure 5 shows RALSTM outperformed previous models with sufficient or limited laptop in-domain data and adapted faster to a new, unseen domain.
The ARED extension introduces RALSTM, improves BLEU and ERR across four NLG domains, extends to unseen domains, and may apply to other encoder-decoder tasks.
